extracted.intended_audience: travellers, art and architecture students, and connoisseurs of Venetian art and buildings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for judging Venetian paintings, sculpture, and buildings (composition, colour, truthfulness to subject, medium-appropriateness, preservation, and taste), written as travel/critical prose about churches, palaces, and works of art in Venice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to religious history versus imaginative abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical manner of representing Scriptural facts which, at this time, was undermining the belief of the facts themselves; e.g., painters representing contemporary figures as Biblical personages and surrounding the Virgin with saints from later centuries to mark the scene as a mere ideality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imaginative abstractions that lose sight of the verities of religious history; balance symbolic/ideal treatment with historical/veracious representation. Consider whether choices (such as dressing Magi as Venetian chamberlains) impair the scene's credibility or reflect modesty/piety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of portraiture within narrative subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting contemporary portraits into historical or sacred scenes can destroy the reality and feeling of the scene (figures introduced 'for the sake of portraiture merely').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include portraiture that distracts from the subject's truth; ensure portrait inclusion serves the scene's conception rather than breaking its veracity or emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical excellence of portraiture and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A work judged 'altogether perfect' when it is carefully and steadily wrought and arranged with consummate skill on a difficult plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the steadiness of execution, carefulness of handling, and skill in arranging complex or elongated formats; consider how technical mastery resolves compositional difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compositional lines and slopes to give unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of detached groups achieved by an overall slope or inclination of lines (e.g., figures arranged so 'all the lines of the picture incline more or less from right to left as they ascend'), and by 'co-ordinates' like upright pillars and horizontal clouds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether compositional diagonals, verticals, and horizontals are used to link groups and create coherent movement and unity across a canvas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour handling: quiet richness and local-tone intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour described as 'very quiet, but rich and deep,' with local tones brought out with intense force and cast shadows subdued; manner closer to Titian than to Tintoret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge colour for balance between restraint and richness, strength of local tones, and controlled use of shadow; compare stylistic affinities (e.g., Titian) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of the sculptural medium (avoid turning sculpture into painting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sculpture round the altar criticized as an 'abuse of the sculptor's art' where every accessory is laboured to turn sculpture into painting (grass, trees, and landscape realized in alto-relievo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpture should respect its medium's strengths: avoid excessive pictorial illusionism in relief that defeats architectural function or reduces sculptural presence to painted imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational qualities of great religious painting
rubrics_metrics.description: John Bellini praised for 'justness of drawing, nobleness of coloring, and perfect manliness of treatment, with the purest religious feeling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess religious paintings for accuracy of drawing, nobility and suitability of colour, manly (i.e., robust, dignified) treatment, and sincere religious feeling rather than mere technical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of technical skill and spiritual/affective content
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist may excel in one technical area (Titian colours better; Leonardo draws better) but lack spiritual feeling or other virtues (Titian 'has not piety'; Leonardo 'has not his colour').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works holistically: strength in drawing, colour, or manner must be accompanied by appropriate feeling, conception, and suitability to subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional conviction and depth of conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Works lacking 'wonder, rapture, or entire devotion' are criticised as having a 'general coldness in expression' — figures merely 'interested and pleased in a mild way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for penetration into the subject, intensity of feeling, and convincing emotional expression; avoid anaemic or merely decorous representations of sacred or dramatic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of execution matching imaginative force
rubrics_metrics.description: Execution that is 'steady and powerful' but not 'affectionate' or 'impetuous' risks mechanical sameness ('would have sunk into a mere mechanist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value execution that adapts to subject demands—occasional impetuosity, tenderness, or abandon may be necessary; purely steady technique without expressive variation is a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of architectural background to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Background architecture can enhance or diminish a painting (e.g., backing Empress Helena with Byzantine architecture might have made the picture far more gorgeous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether architectural elements complement historical authenticity and the mood of the subject; mismatched or anachronistic backgrounds can weaken a composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of social milieu and props
rubrics_metrics.description: Tintoret is noted for always painting the Apostles as poor and ignorant and placing them in rooms befitting lower classes, with homely props (tub, saucepan, bellows) that ground the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether costumes, furnishings, and props are believable for the characters depicted and contribute to the scene's verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and elevation to produce solemnity
rubrics_metrics.description: Solemnity achieved by placing the Saviour at the top of a circle of steps with Apostles kneeling around, producing adoration and astonishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider spatial arrangement, elevation, and the physical relationship of figures in creating ceremonial or solemn effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural honesty and functional appropriateness in architectural ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of the 'base Renaissance' habit of turning keystones into projecting brackets (projecting beyond mouldings) — 'a practice utterly barbarous' that tends to dislocate the arch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer ornament that respects structural logic; avoid decorative devices that are structurally dishonest or that would be problematic under real load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of vulgar or painful decorative practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Filling spandrils with naked figures in alto-relievo 'leaning against the arch' appears as if they might 'slip off' — called a vulgar and painful mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorative schemes should be dignified and appropriate; grotesque or awkward figure-placement in architectural carving is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and harmony of architectural composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of additions that destroy 'euithmia' (harmony) or diminish dignity of a square; the real faults often lie in 'the design of the parts' rather than the number of stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess overall proportions, balance between parts, and relation of a building to its urban context; small disproportionate additions can harm the greater composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful, unaffected portraiture free from vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tintoret's portraits in the Zecca praised for 'quietness and veracity of their unaffected portraiture, and the absolute freedom from all vanity either in the painter or in his subjects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value portraits for truthfulness and lack of self-conscious display; artistic restraint that avoids flattering vanity is commendable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of natural/atmospheric effects (water, rain, light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note the 'dashing of the rain on the pavement' and 'running of the water about the feet of the figures' as significant details; Bonifazio's quails flying across a sunset sky produce a Turneresque effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how convincingly artists render weather, water, and light; skilful atmospheric detail can be a decisive mark of power and naturalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour brilliance and painterly resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Titian's 'Sapienza' praised for the light brilliancy of its colour and resemblance to Paul Veronese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider brilliance, colour harmony, and cross-influences that produce vivid ceiling or large-scale decorative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human feeling and humane sensibility in subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque sculptures (e.g., children's heads tied by the hair) criticized as evidence of lacking 'all human feeling' despite technical skill; contrasted with Ducal Palace treatment where heads emerge naturally from foliage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether technically proficient depiction nevertheless violates humane taste; prefer expressions that preserve dignity and humane sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness of purpose and architectural meaning in sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Some buildings (Miracoli) present refined but 'unmeaning' sculpture; the building becomes 'a small museum of unmeaning, though refined sculpture, than a piece of architecture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculpture should serve architectural purpose and express deliberate intent; avoid decorative refinement without conceptual or structural purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity versus affected archaism
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic doors or traceries that look ancient but exhibit 'bad and spiritless' figures demonstrate the 'Renaissance palsy of imagination' — appearance of antiquity does not guarantee genuine archaic spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish authentic stylistic feeling from mere imitation; value vitality and imaginative power over simulated antiquarian appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste, decency, and the avoidance of grotesque excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Facades like the Ospedaletto ('most monstrous example of the Grotesque Renaissance') representing masses of diseased figures and swollen fruit are condemned as monstrous degradations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess decorative programmes for decency and restraint; grotesque excess that shocks taste is a negative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of preservation and restoration on appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many works 'grievously injured by damp and neglect' or spoilt by 'restoration' (Titian 'restored' now of none value); some pictures require a patient study to decipher meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a work's state of preservation and the impacts of restoration or neglect; acknowledge that some works demand patient, resolute study to reveal their power, while careless restoration can diminish value.
